title: Scientific models
explanation: Keep “simplified representation” together as a phrase. The final sentence explains when simplification is useful; avoid breaking between “features” and “relevant to the question”.
text: A scientific model is a simplified representation of a system. Researchers use models to test explanations and predict outcomes that may be difficult to observe directly. No model includes every detail of the real world. Its value depends on whether the simplifications preserve the features relevant to the question being investigated.

title: Sleep and learning
explanation: The passage says sleep supports study, not that it replaces it. Keep the short third sentence separate from the explanation beginning “Instead”.
text: Learning continues after a student closes a book. During sleep, the brain reorganizes information encountered throughout the day and strengthens some memories. This does not mean that sleep can replace study. Instead, regular rest supports the work already done, making a consistent routine more useful than an occasional night of intensive revision.

explanation: Keep the two observation methods distinct: satellites mainly see the surface, while instruments reach greater depths. Pause before the final sentence about combining methods.
text: Scientists measure ocean temperatures using satellites, floating instruments and research ships. Each method has strengths and limitations. Combining these observations gives researchers a more complete picture than any single method alone.

title: Peer feedback
explanation: Keep “a specific problem” and “explains its effect” connected. The final contrast is between useful detail and simply calling writing good or bad.
text: Giving feedback can help students understand their own writing. When they identify an unclear argument in a classmate’s draft, they practise the same judgement needed to revise their own work. Feedback is most useful when it describes a specific problem and explains its effect, rather than simply calling a piece of writing good or bad.

title: Citizen science
explanation: Include the benefit of wider research coverage and the limits: volunteers need consistent instructions, unusual sightings need checking, and some places receive fewer observations. The bird survey is an example, not the whole argument.
audioText: Citizen science allows members of the public to contribute to scientific research. A familiar example is a bird survey in which volunteers record the species they see in their gardens. Because researchers cannot visit every location themselves, these observations can reveal patterns across a much larger area. However, collecting many observations is not enough on its own. Volunteers need clear instructions so that their records can be compared. Researchers may also ask participants to submit photographs, which help specialists check unusual sightings. Another challenge is that some places attract far more volunteers than others. A city park may be surveyed every week while a remote forest receives little attention. For that reason, researchers must consider where observations came from before drawing conclusions. When these limitations are understood, citizen science can both expand the evidence available to scientists and help communities learn about their environment.
model: The lecture explains how citizen science lets public volunteers extend the reach of research. Bird surveys illustrate the value of observations from many locations. However, volunteers need clear instructions, specialists may need to verify unusual sightings, and researchers must account for places with fewer volunteers. With these limits understood, citizen science can expand evidence and help communities learn about their environment.

title: Retrieval practice
explanation: Distinguish familiarity from recall. Include trying to retrieve information, checking errors afterwards, using achievable questions and spacing attempts across days.
audioText: Many students prepare for examinations by rereading their notes. This feels productive because the information becomes familiar. Familiarity, however, is not the same as being able to recall an idea without help. Retrieval practice involves closing the book and trying to explain what you remember. A student might answer a short question, draw a diagram from memory or teach the concept to a friend. The attempt can reveal gaps that rereading hides. Importantly, checking the answer afterwards is part of the process, because practising an error repeatedly is unlikely to help. Researchers also distinguish a difficult attempt from an impossible one. Questions should require effort while remaining connected to material that the learner has studied. Spacing these attempts across several days can support longer retention than completing them all in one session. The practical lesson is to combine review with opportunities to retrieve information and correct misunderstandings.
model: The lecture contrasts rereading notes with retrieval practice. Familiarity does not guarantee recall, so students can close their books and try to explain an idea, answer questions or draw a diagram from memory. They should check their answers to correct mistakes, use challenging but achievable questions, and space practice across days to support longer retention.

title: Library opening hours
explanation: Keep the three positions separate: later access for working students, concern about staffing costs, and a limited exam-period trial with attendance checks. The speakers have not agreed to open the whole library later permanently.
audioText: Speaker one. I think the library should stay open later. Students who work during the day often have no quiet place to study in the evening. Last week I arrived after my shift and had only an hour before the building closed. Extending the hours would make a real difference to people like me. Speaker two. I understand that, but keeping the whole building open means paying for security and other staff. The university has a limited budget. I would rather protect the daytime services than reduce them to pay for a few extra hours at night. We should find out how many students would actually use the space. Speaker three. Perhaps we could try opening just the ground floor later during the exam period. That would provide a quiet area without the expense of running every floor. We could count attendance and ask students whether the service helped. Then the university could make a decision based on evidence rather than guesses.

title: Community gardens
explanation: Connect the gardens’ food and social benefits with the need for fair responsibilities and clear rules. A summary about growing food alone misses the passage’s main qualification.
text: Community gardens are often promoted as a way to grow fresh food, but their social value may be just as important. Residents who previously had little contact can meet while caring for shared plots. Experienced gardeners pass on practical knowledge, and newcomers gain an informal reason to spend time outdoors. These benefits do not arise automatically. A garden that has no clear arrangements for watering, tool storage or access may become a source of disagreement. Some communities address this problem by agreeing on simple rules at the start and reviewing them each season. Others appoint a coordinator to make sure tasks are shared fairly. Successful gardens therefore depend on social organization as well as suitable soil and sunlight. Their value lies in the combination of food production, cooperation and opportunities for local residents to learn from one another.
model: Community gardens can produce food and strengthen local relationships, but they need fair responsibilities and clear rules to turn a shared growing space into a lasting community resource.

title: Digital archives
explanation: Include wider access and protection of originals, then the work needed to maintain a reliable digital collection. Do not imply that digitization preserves everything or replaces physical archives completely.
text: Digitizing historical documents can make them available to readers who cannot travel to an archive. High-quality images also reduce the need to handle fragile originals. Yet the process involves more than photographing pages. Each item needs a description that helps readers discover it, and the files must be stored in formats that future systems can open. Handwritten words may be difficult for automated recognition software to interpret, so a searchable version often requires human checking. There are also choices about which records to digitize first. Popular collections may attract attention while less familiar material remains inaccessible. For these reasons, a digital archive should be understood as a carefully maintained selection rather than a complete replacement for a physical collection. Long-term access depends on continued investment in description, preservation and thoughtful decisions about whose histories are represented.
model: Digital archives widen access and protect fragile documents, but reliable discovery and long-term preservation require accurate descriptions, human checking and careful selection of the records included.

title: University and practical skills

model: Academic knowledge: explain how theory and critical reasoning help graduates solve unfamiliar problems. Practical skills: discuss applying ideas through placements, projects or laboratory work. Your position: explain the balance you favour and give a concrete example. End by connecting that balance to the role you think universities should serve.

title: Cooler roofs
explanation: Include how reflective roofs reduce cooling demand, why colder climates may benefit less, and why cities test materials and maintenance costs across seasons. Do not present one roof design as suitable everywhere.
audioText: Today I want to discuss why cities are experimenting with cooler roofs. A conventional dark roof absorbs much of the sunlight that reaches it, which can increase the temperature inside a building. A pale roof reflects more sunlight and may reduce the need for air conditioning during hot weather. However, it would be misleading to say that one roof design works equally well everywhere. In a cold region, reflecting winter sunlight could increase heating needs. The material also matters because dust and weathering can reduce its reflectivity over time. Some local governments are testing several surfaces before recommending a particular approach. They measure indoor temperatures, energy use and maintenance costs across different seasons. The main lesson is that a promising technology still needs to be evaluated in context. A cooler roof can be useful, but its overall benefit depends on climate, building design and how well the surface is maintained.
model: Reflective roofs can lower indoor temperatures and reduce cooling demand by reflecting sunlight. However, their benefits vary with climate, building design and maintenance, and they may increase heating needs in colder regions. Cities are therefore testing materials across seasons, comparing temperatures, energy consumption and costs before recommending solutions suitable for local conditions.

title: Public spaces
explanation: The best summary connects practical features with users’ needs. The speaker says small spaces can work well, so size alone does not determine success. Photographs cannot replace observing how people use the space.
audioText: A successful public space does not have to be large. A small square with shade, seating and safe access can attract more people than an impressive plaza with nowhere to rest. Designers should observe how different groups use the area at different times. For example, a route that works well for commuters in the morning may need better lighting for evening visitors. The important point is to judge the space by the needs of its users rather than its appearance in an architectural photograph.
options: Public spaces should be judged by how well they serve people, with practical features and attention to different patterns of use.
Large plazas are always more popular than small squares because they look impressive.
Architectural photographs provide enough evidence to decide whether a public space is successful.

title: Food labels
explanation: The best summary combines accuracy, comparable measures and understandable presentation. The recording says people may need education; it does not propose removing all numbers.
audioText: A food label can contain accurate information without being easy to understand. If serving sizes differ between products, shoppers may find it difficult to compare them quickly. Displaying values per one hundred grams can help, but consumers still need to know what each measure means. Researchers therefore study both the accuracy of labels and how people interpret them. Clear design and education may need to work together. More information alone does not guarantee a better decision.
options: Useful food labels need accurate information, comparable measures and presentation that consumers can understand.
Every shopper understands food labels, so education is unnecessary.
Removing all numerical information is the only way to improve food labels.

title: A changed seminar
explanation: The seminar moves from the science building to room twelve in the library. The time stays at three, the article is unchanged, and students do not need to register again.
audioText: This is a message for students attending Thursday’s seminar. We had planned to meet in the science building, but repair work means that room is unavailable. title: Research interviews
explanation: A pilot interview checks whether questions are understood as intended. It does not teach preferred answers, avoid collecting information or replace the main interviews.
audioText: When planning interviews, researchers should allow time to test their questions. A question that seems clear to its writer may confuse someone else. In a pilot interview, the researcher can ask the participant to explain how they understood the wording. This does not mean training participants to give a preferred answer. It means checking whether the question invites the kind of information the study needs. Revising ambiguous wording before the main interviews can save considerable time later.

title: Long-term planning
explanation: New homes and workplaces can change travel demand, so “exactly the same” completes the assumption planners should avoid. The other endings do not fit this contrast.
audioText: When a town designs a new transport network, it has to think beyond the number of passengers travelling today. Housing developments may change where people live, and new workplaces may change where they need to go. A route that appears unnecessary now could become important in a few years.
